title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
authors: Mickaël Delcey, Cyril Regan, Masaki Fuchiwaki, Yoann Cheny
abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.

infographic.key_insight: A data-free, continuous-time PINN produces cylinder vortex shedding, while pressure matching plus a hidden incompressibility constraint improves consistency across training windows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports physics-only prediction of unsteady wakes and smoother aerodynamic loads across successive training windows.
method: Train over successive time windows without reference data or temporal discretization.
Break wake symmetry with an analytical, divergence-free initial condition.
Match junction pressure and penalize ∇·∂ₜv = 0, using the momentum equation to evaluate ∂ₜv.
infographic.evidence_signal: At Re=100, Strouhal number and mean drag agree with same-domain OpenFOAM results within 0.5%; the consistency remedy reduces lift-coefficient jumps 20-fold over five shedding periods.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the reported Re=100 cylinder case and five-period consistency evaluation; broader flow-regime robustness remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows

title: SPARK: Spectral Preconditioned Analytic Residual Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for incompressible Navier Stokes equations
authors: Dathi Rajasekhar, Thien-Tam Nguyen, Trung Bao Le
abstract: We propose Spectral Jet KAN (SJ-KAN) to reduce the cost of differentiation and the network complexity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations. The input coordinates are embedded through Chebyshev bases whose spatial derivatives are known in closed form, and all differentiation matrices are computed once for the collocation points before training. A single linear layer compresses the Chebyshev bases into a few latent features, and a single nonlinear Chebyshev Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (CKAN) layer maps these features to the physical variables. Because the basis derivatives are known in advance and the compression is linear, the spatial derivatives in the NS equations are carried through the network analytically by a fixed sequence of matrix products and elementwise operations. Automatic differentiation (AD) is used only in backpropagation, to compute the gradients of the loss with respect to the network weights. We examine three variants of SJ-KAN (JetKAN, JetKAN-F, JetKAN-H), which differ in how the output layer maps the latent features to the physical variables. All variants are tested on the Taylor-Green vortex and on the lid driven cavity at Reynolds numbers Re = 100, 1000, 5000 and 10,000. The results are compared with a KAN that uses AD (PIKAN) and with a standard PINN. The SJ-KAN variants reach comparable or better accuracy than both, with up to 47 times fewer parameters and up to 8.2 times faster training per epoch. SJ-KAN also solves the lid driven cavity flow at Re = 10,000 without any reference data and with fewer than 9,000 trainable parameters. These results show that analytic derivative propagation, a small spectral input layer and a single KAN layer give a faster and simpler solver than methods based on AD, also for flows at high Reynolds numbers.

infographic.key_insight: SJ-KAN propagates spatial derivatives analytically through a compact spectral network, achieving comparable or better accuracy than PINN and PIKAN baselines with substantially lower computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could make physics-informed incompressible flow simulation more affordable, including high-Reynolds-number cavity flows without reference data.
method: Embed coordinates in Chebyshev bases and precompute basis derivatives at collocation points.
Compress the bases linearly into latent features, then map them to physical variables with one nonlinear Chebyshev KAN layer.
Evaluate PDE derivatives analytically; use automatic differentiation only for loss gradients with respect to weights.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on the Taylor–Green vortex and lid-driven cavity at Re = 100–10,000 report up to 47× fewer parameters and 8.2× faster training per epoch than the baselines; the Re = 10,000 cavity was solved without reference data using fewer than 9,000 parameters.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish performance on complex geometries or turbulent flows, and faster epochs do not necessarily imply shorter time to convergence.
infographic.paper_title: SPARK: Spectral Preconditioned Analytic Residual Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for incompressible Navier Stokes equations

title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes
authors: Ao Cheng, Lei Zhang, Guowei He
abstract: Classical dimensional analysis defines admissible dimensionless representations but does not determine which combinations capture the dominant physical dependence, whether it changes across physical regimes, or when dependent-variable rescaling is required. We present AI Buckingham, an agentic framework for autonomous dimensionless discovery from natural-language descriptions of physical problems and observational data. It couples reasoning and planning by a large language model (LLM) with predefined symbolic and numerical tools. Literature-based knowledge retrieval supports dimensional checking, gradient-based clustering identifies physical regimes, and mutual information provides an objective, reparameterization-invariant criterion for identifying dominant dimensionless groups. Explicit numerical criteria determine the group count and assess simplification. Across ten physical systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, AI Buckingham recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings. For the longstanding challenge of predicting turbulent drag on rough surfaces, it identifies informative reparameterizations of surface statistics that improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates for engineering-oriented drag modelling.

infographic.key_insight: AI Buckingham combines LLM-guided reasoning with numerical tools to discover dominant dimensionless groups and how their scaling changes across physical regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For turbulent flow over rough surfaces, informative reparameterizations of surface statistics improve equivalent sand-grain roughness estimates used in engineering drag models.
method: Use literature retrieval and dimensional checks to constrain admissible representations.
Identify physical regimes with gradient-based clustering and rank dimensionless groups using mutual information.
Apply explicit numerical criteria to select group count and assess simplification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten systems spanning fluid dynamics, magnetohydrodynamics, thermal convection and additive manufacturing, the framework recovers established similarity representations and resolves regime-dependent scalings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify predictive gains or establish generalization to unseen roughness geometries and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: AI Buckingham: Agentic Discovery of Dimensionless Scaling Laws Across Physical Regimes

title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators
authors: Guodan Dong, Qi Qian, Feifei Xue, Jianhua Qin, Chang Xu, Wenzhong Shen
abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed Fourier neural operator reconstructs unsteady 3D floating-wind-turbine wakes from two observation planes and transfers learned wake dynamics across turbine scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms with limited wake measurements.
method: Generate fixed and surge–pitch wake data using large-eddy simulation coupled with an actuator line model.
Combine 4D spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization.
Train on 5 MW turbine cases and transfer-learn to a 22 MW turbine.
infographic.evidence_signal: In simulation-based tests, 10% planar sampling nearly matched dense-sampling accuracy (relative L2 error 0.0689 versus 0.0684), while transfer learning reduced 22 MW streamwise-velocity error at St = 0.6 by 36% versus zero-shot inference.
infographic.watch_item: Fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped, and the reported results establish performance on simulated rather than field-measured wakes.
infographic.paper_title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators

title: Physics-informed neural networks for strong normal shocks in kinetic relaxation models and the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation
authors: Ehsan Roohi
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic equations have mostly been applied near equilibrium and judged by density, velocity and temperature. Here a network trained on the kinetic equation alone, with no reference data in the loss, solves steady normal shock waves and is assessed in eight fields: density, velocity, temperature, heat flux, stress, a third-order moment and two fourth-order moments. The network corrects a mixture of the two end-state Maxwellians by an unbounded, signed factor with exact inflow; the loss, the residual in three norms with conservation terms, is minimised by Adam and a self-scaled quasi-Newton method with continuation in the Mach number. For the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation at Mach 8, in a comparison made once after reference-free tests, the largest relative $L^2$ difference from direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) over the eight fields is 0.19 per cent; at Mach 10 it is 0.34 per cent. The distribution function itself agrees with the reference over six decades in velocity space. For the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model, a blind prediction at Mach 50 gives density, velocity and temperature to about 0.1 per cent and exposes a loss of accuracy confined to the two fourth-order moments. Its origin is identified as a passive reduced distribution that carries little weight in the loss; with a larger weight on that distribution and a longer optimisation, both moments are within 3.2 per cent of the discrete-velocity solution up to Mach 70 and 7.1 per cent at Mach 100. The Shakhov model is solved to Mach 20 and a Rykov-type model of nitrogen to Mach 15.

infographic.key_insight: Reference-free PINNs resolve strong kinetic shock waves with high accuracy, but higher-order moments reveal errors that bulk flow fields can miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a promising route to predicting strongly nonequilibrium gas flows relevant to high-speed aerospace applications.
method: Learn a signed correction to an end-state Maxwellian mixture with exact inflow conditions.
Minimise kinetic residuals in three norms plus conservation terms, without reference data in the loss.
Combine Adam, self-scaled quasi-Newton optimisation and Mach-number continuation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight fields, the largest relative L2 difference from DSMC for hard-sphere Boltzmann shocks was 0.19% at Mach 8 and 0.34% at Mach 10.
infographic.watch_item: High-Mach BGK fourth-order moments required loss reweighting and longer optimisation; their errors remained up to 7.1% at Mach 100.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-informed neural networks for strong normal shocks in kinetic relaxation models and the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation

title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets
authors: Shreyash Gulati, Sven R. Walsberg, Timothy W. Nearhood, Jeffrey D. Moore
abstract: In the current work, the investigators used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to investigate water flow and cavitation in single-liquid injectors with sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. The k-ω Shear Stress Transport (SST) turbulence model was used along with the Zwart-Gerber-Belamri (ZGB) cavitation model and the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. The CFD predictions for the volumetric flow rate were validated against existing experimental data for the sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. Pressure drops ranging between 0.07 MPa and 0.59 MPa were considered along with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2, 5, and 10. Strong cavitation was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop larger than 0.2 MPa. A hydraulic flip was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop of 0.59 MPa, which was consistent with the findings from the previous experimental study. Cavitation inception was observed for the chamfered orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and pressure drops larger than 0.2 MPa. For the sharp-edged orifice inlet with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2 and 10, a strong cavitation was observed inside the orifice.

infographic.key_insight: In CFD simulations at L/D = 5 and pressure drops above 0.2 MPa, sharp-edged inlets showed strong cavitation while chamfered inlets showed cavitation inception.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Inlet geometry and orifice length-to-diameter ratio are important design considerations for controlling cavitation and hydraulic flip in liquid injectors.
method: CFD using k–ω SST turbulence, Zwart–Gerber–Belamri cavitation, and Volume of Fluid models.
Compared sharp-edged and chamfered water-injector inlets.
Studied pressure drops of 0.07–0.59 MPa and L/D ratios of 2, 5, and 10.
infographic.evidence_signal: Volumetric flow predictions were validated against existing experiments, and hydraulic flip at L/D = 5 and 0.59 MPa for the sharp-edged inlet agreed with prior experimental findings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation errors, limiting assessment of predictive accuracy beyond the reported agreement.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets

title: Dopamine: A Cartesian grid large-eddy-simulation framework for coastal ocean modelling of free-surface waves
authors: Akshay Patil
abstract: We present a Cartesian staggered-grid large-eddy simulation framework for modelling coastal ocean waves using the Dopamine solver. The framework combines a geometric volume-of-fluid method for simulating free-surface wave evolution with one-way-coupled Lagrangian point-particle tracking for heavy and buoyant particles. A ghost-cell immersed-boundary method represents stationary solid boundaries, including the seabed and coastal obstacles, and their interaction with free-surface waves. The framework includes the Vreman and anisotropic minimum-dissipation (AMD) sub-grid-scale models for simulating near-wall turbulence. Comparisons with analytical solutions and established experimental and numerical benchmarks illustrate the framework's ability to reproduce wave dynamics and particle motion. The results provide promising insights into the framework's capabilities for coastal ocean modelling applications focused on investigating small-scale turbulent physics using a low-numerical-dissipation approach. The solver runs on multi-CPU architectures, with two-fluid strong- and weak-scaling efficiencies at 512 ranks relative to 64 ranks of up to 77% and 73%, respectively, and a single-GPGPU build has been verified against the CPU solver.

infographic.key_insight: Dopamine combines Cartesian-grid large-eddy simulation with free-surface and particle modelling to study small-scale turbulent physics in coastal waves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports investigation of wave interactions with seabeds, coastal obstacles, and heavy or buoyant particles.
method: Geometric volume-of-fluid wave tracking on a staggered Cartesian grid.
Ghost-cell immersed boundaries for stationary solids and one-way-coupled Lagrangian point particles.
Vreman and anisotropic minimum-dissipation sub-grid-scale turbulence models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical, experimental, and numerical comparisons support wave and particle predictions; two-fluid scaling efficiencies reach 77% strong and 73% weak at 512 CPU ranks relative to 64, and a single-GPGPU build was verified against the CPU solver.
infographic.watch_item: One-way particle coupling omits particle feedback on the flow, limiting applicability when particle loading materially affects wave or turbulence dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Dopamine: A Cartesian grid large-eddy-simulation framework for coastal ocean modelling of free-surface waves

title: Energy cascade spectrum in wave turbulence of a two-dimensional quantum fluid
authors: Ying Zhu, Jason Laurie, Giorgio Krstulovic, Sergey Nazarenko
abstract: In the two-dimensional (2D) Gross-Pitaevskii model for a Bose gas, the naive dimensional non-equilibrium wave-turbulence power-law prediction for the direct energy cascade coincides with thermal equilibrium and therefore carries no energy flux. We resolve this degeneracy by deriving a logarithmically corrected spectrum that supports a positive, constant energy flux toward small scales. A systematic asymptotic expansion of the wave-kinetic collision integral determines the logarithmic exponent to be 1/3, while the small-scale dissipation scale sets the upper cutoff in the logarithmic correction. Regularization of a marginal infrared divergence at the forcing scale yields an estimate of the spectral prefactor for asymptotically well-separated forcing and dissipation scales. Simulations of the Gross-Pitaevskii and wave-kinetic equations support the predicted spectral shape. Over finite spectral ranges, the correction produces apparent power laws steeper than the dimensional prediction, offering a possible explanation for the steep spectra observed in 2D Bose gas experiments. Our approach provides a systematic framework for constructing wave turbulent cascade spectra when the power-law prediction is degenerate with thermodynamic equilibrium.

infographic.key_insight: A logarithmic correction with exponent 1/3 enables a constant, positive energy flux toward small scales in 2D quantum-fluid wave turbulence, where the naive power law instead describes thermal equilibrium.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The corrected spectrum can guide interpretation and numerical modeling of energy transfer in two-dimensional Bose gases.
method: Derive the logarithmic correction through an asymptotic expansion of the wave-kinetic collision integral.
Set the logarithmic upper cutoff using the small-scale dissipation scale.
Regularize the marginal infrared divergence at the forcing scale to estimate the spectral prefactor.
infographic.evidence_signal: Gross-Pitaevskii and wave-kinetic simulations support the predicted spectral shape, whose finite-range appearance may explain steep spectra observed in 2D Bose gas experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The prefactor estimate assumes asymptotically well-separated forcing and dissipation scales, so finite-scale applications require caution.
infographic.paper_title: Energy cascade spectrum in wave turbulence of a two-dimensional quantum fluid

title: BridgeSRDA: Efficient Probabilistic Super-Resolution Data Assimilation with Forecast-Informed Stochastic Interpolants
authors: Aditya Sai Pranith Ayapilla, Yuki Yasuda, Ryo Onishi
abstract: High-resolution ensemble data assimilation is computationally demanding because it requires repeated forecasts and updates of many flow states. We introduce BridgeSRDA, a probabilistic super-resolution data assimilation framework that combines low-resolution numerical forecasts with sparse, noisy observations to generate high-resolution analysis windows. A neural network learns forecast-informed stochastic transport, which is sampled to produce an ensemble of reconstructions. Each current analysis initializes the next low-resolution forecast, while the same window provides retrospective reconstructions and short-range nowcasts. We evaluate BridgeSRDA over ten independently initialized trajectories of a three-dimensional quasi-geostrophic flow in a narrow-jet regime different from training. At the training observation spacing, BridgeSRDA approaches the mean and structural reconstruction accuracy of a high-resolution local ensemble transform Kalman filter and reduces the mean absolute error ratio by approximately 32.5% relative to deterministic four-dimensional SRDA. With 30 ensemble members, BridgeSRDA requires approximately 17 s per analysis, compared with 31 s for the filter under the recorded conditions. Ten members reduce the cost to approximately 6.6 s with little change in mean accuracy, though fine-scale accuracy and interval coverage are affected. BridgeSRDA achieves a competitive continuous ranked probability score, but its ensembles are underdispersed: nominal 90% intervals contain approximately 62% of reference values. Boundary spread artifacts and reduced skill under sparser observations also warrant attention. These results demonstrate the potential of forecast-informed stochastic transport for probabilistic data assimilation, while highlighting the need to improve uncertainty calibration and robustness to changing observation networks.

infographic.key_insight: BridgeSRDA combines low-resolution forecasts with sparse, noisy observations to generate probabilistic high-resolution flow reconstructions at lower cost than a high-resolution ensemble filter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could make ensemble flow-state estimation more affordable while providing retrospective reconstructions and short-range nowcasts.
method: Train a neural network to learn forecast-informed stochastic transport.
Sample high-resolution analysis ensembles conditioned on low-resolution forecasts and observations.
Use each current analysis to initialize the next low-resolution forecast.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten independently initialized 3D quasi-geostrophic trajectories in an unseen narrow-jet regime, BridgeSRDA reduced the mean absolute error ratio by approximately 32.5% versus deterministic 4D-SRDA at training observation spacing; 30-member analyses took approximately 17 s versus 31 s for the high-resolution filter.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertainty remains undercalibrated: nominal 90% intervals covered approximately 62% of reference values, with boundary spread artifacts and reduced skill under sparser observations.
infographic.paper_title: BridgeSRDA: Efficient Probabilistic Super-Resolution Data Assimilation with Forecast-Informed Stochastic Interpolants

title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field
authors: Parv Khurana, Benet Eiximeno, Alexandra Liosi, Spencer Sherwin, Athanasios Chatzopoulos, Julien Hoessler
abstract: The aerodynamic performance of motorsport vehicles relies on understanding the unsteady flow dynamics around complex geometries at high Reynolds numbers. Extracting the dominant 3D coherent structures from high-fidelity simulations is often intractable due to the high dimensionality of the state-space, and standard modal decompositions, such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), do not give interpretable meaning to the temporal dynamics of the modes. This study demonstrates a scalable POD and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method, implemented in the open-source pyLOM framework, that can identify coherent structures and their temporal dynamics in high-fidelity simulations of Formula 1 aerodynamics, specifically the Imperial Front Wing (IFW), a publicly available benchmark based on the McLaren MP4-17D, at Reynolds number $Re = 2.2 \times 10^5$. DMD is applied to large eddy simulation (LES) results of the flow field that is resolved using spectral/hp element method via Nektar++, producing $49.72 \times 10^6$ degrees of freedom at polynomial order p=4. The simulation captures four dominant vortical structures (endplate, canard, main, and footplate), with time-averaged force coefficients showing 2.24% and 2.87% differences in $C_L$ and $C_D$ compared to the reference data. DMD extracts the frequencies, amplitudes and damping ratios of the coherent structures, and modes at chord-based Strouhal numbers of 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 are associated, through point-probe spectra, with the main-element laminar separation bubble, canard vortex core pulsation and endplate vortex meander, respectively. The DMD allows for both a model reduction technique and a compression scheme, here reducing approximately 6 TB of snapshots to 200 GB of modal data.

infographic.key_insight: Scalable modal decomposition reveals dominant coherent flow structures and their temporal dynamics around a Formula 1 front wing while compressing approximately 6 TB of snapshots into 200 GB of modal data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Identifying characteristic frequencies of wing-flow instabilities can support aerodynamic diagnosis and reduced-order modeling for motorsport design.
method: Simulate the Imperial Front Wing at Re = 2.2 × 10^5 using spectral/hp-element LES in Nektar++.
Apply scalable POD and DMD through the open-source pyLOM framework.
Use point-probe spectra to associate DMD modes with specific flow mechanisms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulation uses 49.72 million degrees of freedom, reports lift and drag coefficient differences of 2.24% and 2.87% from reference data, and links chord-based Strouhal numbers 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 to distinct flow mechanisms.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract demonstrates one geometry and Reynolds number; transferability to other operating conditions and reduced-order predictive accuracy remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field

title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data
authors: John Mathew Quinlan
abstract: Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) fits one constant linear operator to a sequence of snapshots. When the dynamics, or the view of them, vary periodically, as in a parametrically excited flow or a rotating structure seen in a fixed plane, no such operator exists, and stability is decided by the Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map over one period. In the paper that introduced DMD, Schmid observed that snapshots sampled at the period of an oscillatory flow would identify the Floquet matrix. We develop that observation into a method and analyze it. The Floquet decomposition (FD) applies DMD to fixed-rate data subsampled once per period; the ensemble Floquet decomposition (EFD) stacks the snapshots of each period into one column, giving one set of multipliers and phase-resolved modes. For linear time-periodic systems both are exact: FD when the measurement at one instant determines the state, EFD when the measurements over one period do---so EFD succeeds with partial measurements. EFD and Hankel (delay-embedded) DMD use the same data matrix with different shifts between columns. With $p$ samples per period, Hankel-DMD returns each Floquet mode as a carrier with sidebands, a comb of $p$-th roots of its multiplier, which the period shift collapses onto the multiplier. The methods are verified against known multipliers; outside their hypotheses, on nonlinear or noisy data, the estimated moduli are biased and are not decay rates. Measurements of velocity, scalars, and acoustic pressure in a swirl-stabilized combustor illustrate the choice of period, rank, and data scaling.

infographic.key_insight: Period-shifted snapshot analysis recovers Floquet multipliers and time-periodic modes, revealing stability in systems that a single constant DMD operator cannot represent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports stability analysis of periodically varying flows and measurements, including combustor dynamics and rotating structures.
method: FD applies DMD to snapshots subsampled once per period.
EFD stacks each period’s snapshots to recover shared multipliers and phase-resolved modes.
EFD can handle partial measurements when observations over one period determine the state.
infographic.evidence_signal: The methods are verified against known multipliers and illustrated using velocity, scalar, and acoustic-pressure measurements from a swirl-stabilized combustor.
infographic.watch_item: Exactness requires linear time-periodic dynamics and sufficient observability; nonlinear or noisy data can bias multiplier moduli, which should not be interpreted as decay rates.
infographic.paper_title: Floquet Decomposition: Floquet Multipliers and Time-Periodic Modes from Period-Sampled Snapshot Data

title: A centered finite-volume method with explicit pressure relaxation for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows
authors: Shintaro Matsushita, Suhas S. Jain, Andrei G. Fedorov, Tetsuya Suekane
abstract: We present a non-dissipative centered finite-volume method for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows. The method couples kinetic-energy-preserving advection to conservative diffuse-interface regularization and explicit pressure relaxation on structured collocated grids. To control excessive phase-mass outflow when neighboring cells have different intrinsic densities, we construct phase-mass fluxes using harmonic face densities. This connects phase-volume and phase-mass transport without altering the advective kinetic-energy identity, yielding a sufficient positivity condition and an inverse-density transport identity at finite velocity divergence. To retain the benefit of low-dissipation transport in the coupled calculation, a pressure-increment formulation incorporates the existing pressure gradient in the predictor. Compatible cell and face operators give a conditional energy estimate for additional pressure iterations, while fully discrete budgets separate advection, predictor pressure work, and the final correction. In inviscid homogeneous isotropic turbulence on $128^3$ cells, the relative kinetic-energy change remains below $1.2\times10^{-7}$ in magnitude at $t^*=8$ in both single-phase and density-ratio-$1000$ two-phase calculations. Matched upwind calculations retain only $3.60\%$ and $30.72\%$ of their initial energies, respectively. Shear layers, cavities, rising bubbles, and dam breaks demonstrate applicability to incompressible-regime flows. In a three-dimensional dam break, harmonic averaging retains positive phase masses where arithmetic averaging produces negative values. With centered advection, a prescribed subgrid-scale stress supplies the principal dissipation. The local pressure algorithm and collocated finite-volume form support future large-scale multiphase large-eddy simulation on GPUs with adaptive mesh refinement.

infographic.key_insight: Centered finite-volume transport with explicit pressure relaxation nearly preserves kinetic energy in weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows, while harmonic face densities help maintain positive phase masses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports low-dissipation multiphase turbulence simulation and offers a foundation for future GPU-based large-eddy simulation with adaptive mesh refinement.
method: Couple kinetic-energy-preserving centered advection with conservative diffuse-interface regularization.
Use harmonic face densities to connect phase-volume and phase-mass transport.
Apply pressure-increment relaxation with compatible cell and face operators on structured collocated grids.
infographic.evidence_signal: In inviscid turbulence on 128³ cells at t*=8, relative kinetic-energy changes stayed below 1.2×10⁻⁷ in magnitude for single-phase and density-ratio-1000 two-phase cases; matched upwind runs retained only 3.60% and 30.72% of initial energy, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Phase-mass positivity and the additional-pressure-iteration energy estimate are conditional; centered transport relies on a prescribed subgrid-scale stress for principal dissipation.
infographic.paper_title: A centered finite-volume method with explicit pressure relaxation for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows

title: Basin-Scale Nonlinear Dynamics of Thermohaline Ocean Circulation. Part I: Theory
authors: Conner W. Lester, Dylan E. McNamara, Till J. W. Wagner
abstract: Earth's thermohaline ocean circulation may support multiple equilibria and abrupt transitions. Similar bifurcation structures for different ocean models suggest common underlying dynamics across the model hierarchy. Here we propose a unifying framework from tracer conservation, in which surface fluxes are balanced by dissipative and advective tracer transport. We express this flux balance through a large-scale tracer gradient and a transport efficiency that measures how strongly circulation displaces the tracer field from its no-flow "conductive" state. The flux balance quantifies the transport contributions that sustain each circulation state and give rise to abrupt transitions. In a three-dimensional ocean-basin model, we find nonlinear salinity advection dominates the collapse threshold and linear dissipation dominates the recovery threshold. Temperature has additional dissipation from surface restoring, making thermal fluxes more dissipation-dominated than salinity fluxes. The tracer contrasts and boundary layers that a given circulation generates produce distinct transport regimes, approximately quadratic in circulation strength for weak flow and linear for strong flow. With a simple circulation closure, the flux balance reduces to longstanding box-model bifurcation results for the weak and strong flow regimes. Thus, by expressing thermohaline bifurcations through basin-scale transport, this framework connects box-model insight to the continuous equations. Furthermore, as this framework exposes the transport processes that balance a changing forcing, it provides constraints on a thermohaline ocean state and its trend toward tipping that overturning strength alone does not. In Part II, we develop flux-balance closures to forecast such tipping points.

infographic.key_insight: A basin-scale tracer-flux framework links thermohaline circulation tipping to the balance between nonlinear advection and linear dissipation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Transport-budget diagnostics could improve ocean-model stability assessment by revealing proximity to tipping that overturning strength alone cannot show.
method: Derive a tracer-conservation balance between surface fluxes, dissipation, and advection.
Describe transport using large-scale tracer gradients and efficiency relative to a no-flow conductive state.
Evaluate a three-dimensional basin model and connect weak- and strong-flow regimes to box-model bifurcations.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the three-dimensional basin model, nonlinear salinity advection dominates the collapse threshold, while linear dissipation dominates recovery.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports idealized basin-model results, not validation against observed ocean tipping; forecasting closures are deferred to Part II.
infographic.paper_title: Basin-Scale Nonlinear Dynamics of Thermohaline Ocean Circulation. Part I: Theory

title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids
authors: Anantharaman Sekharipuram Viswanathan, Dipankar Bhattacharya
abstract: Superfluids, in a spinning-down container with pinning centres, exhibit sudden collective migration of quantized vortices. The onset, progress, and termination of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we show that: 1) the first exodus of vortices occurs when a sector of the vortex array, having a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall; 2) driven by this exodus, the superfluid flow near the boundary continually decreases in strength and arrests the exit; and 3) the resultant depletion region has well-defined dimensions---governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, the container size, and the initial rotation rate---that limit the angular momentum transferred to the container. We conclude by discussing the relevance to pulsar glitches.

infographic.key_insight: Collective vortex escape in a pinned, spinning-down superfluid weakens boundary flow until the escape self-arrests, limiting angular momentum transfer.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings connect pinning thresholds, container size, and initial rotation to bounded angular momentum release in rotating superfluids.
method: Identify the minimum opening angle of a near-wall sector vacated at the onset of collective vortex escape.
Track how vortex escape reduces boundary flow and arrests further exit.
Relate depletion-region dimensions to critical unpinning velocity, container size, and initial rotation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an onset criterion and well-defined depletion-region dimensions, but provides no quantitative results or validation details.
infographic.watch_item: Relevance to pulsar glitches is discussed, but applicability beyond the studied container and pinning conditions is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids

title: Electrostatic effects on settling cloud droplets: from pair collisions to size distribution evolution
authors: Pijush Patra, John S. Wettlaufer
abstract: We investigate how droplet charge and a uniform vertical electric field influence collisions between cloud droplets settling in still air and how these collisions shape the droplet size distribution. We compute collision efficiencies by analyzing the relative trajectories of pairs of spherical, conducting droplets, accounting for droplet inertia, exact hydrodynamic, electrostatic, and van der Waals forces. The hydrodynamic interactions are based on exact two-body solutions for Stokes flow with interfacial mobility and internal circulation. In the absence of an applied electric field, collisions between like-charged droplets are suppressed, whereas collisions between oppositely-charged droplets are enhanced. A vertical electric field promotes collisions between uncharged droplets through induced polarization and, when sufficiently strong, can overcome the repulsion between like-charged droplets. When the larger droplet has a radius of $10$ or $20μ$m raising the electric field strength from $5\times10^{4}$ to $3\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ can enhance the collision efficiency of uncharged droplet pairs by an order of magnitude. Depending on droplet size and field strength, for oppositely charged pairs, an applied electric field can either enhance or suppress collisions relative to the zero-field case. Using collision kernels computed from droplet pair trajectories, we solve the stochastic collection equation with a flux method on a two-dimensional grid that resolves droplet mass and charge. For an initial mean droplet radius of $10μ$m , by $40$ min in every electrified case the large-droplet mode of the mass spectrum reaches a larger radius than in the hydrodynamic reference case. This suggests that electrostatic interactions can hasten warm rain initiation by accelerating droplet growth through collision and coalescence.

infographic.key_insight: Droplet charge and vertical electric fields can accelerate collision-driven cloud droplet growth, potentially hastening warm rain initiation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Charge- and field-dependent collision kernels could improve cloud microphysics models that predict droplet growth and rainfall onset.
method: Compute pair trajectories with droplet inertia, exact hydrodynamic interactions, electrostatic forces, and van der Waals forces.
Derive collision efficiencies for conducting droplets across charge states and vertical electric fields.
Evolve droplet distributions using a stochastic collection equation on a mass–charge grid.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show an order-of-magnitude increase in uncharged-pair collision efficiency as the field rises from 5×10⁴ to 3×10⁵ V/m for larger-droplet radii of 10 or 20 μm; by 40 minutes, every electrified case has a larger-radius large-droplet mode than the hydrodynamic reference.
infographic.watch_item: The model considers spherical conducting droplets settling in still air, so applicability to turbulent clouds requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Electrostatic effects on settling cloud droplets: from pair collisions to size distribution evolution

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
authors: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

infographic.key_insight: RheOFormer’s viscoplastic-flow prediction improves with logarithmic velocity representations, gradient-aware losses, and a few training cases covering missing physical regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These remedies support more reliable, data-efficient CFD surrogates for flows containing both yielded regions and low-gradient, unyielded plugs.
method: Evaluate RheOFormer on steady Bingham channel flow across dataset structures, value ranges, and input representations.
Use logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware losses to improve plug-region predictions.
Add strategically selected training cases to reduce extrapolation errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved accuracy in challenging regimes and accurate steady-state prediction from one partially developed snapshot, outperforming simply copying the input.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to a simple channel geometry and Bingham constitutive model; generalization to more complex flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows

title: Pressure demand and solute replacement in a collagen-plugged bioreactor
authors: Mohammad Mehedi Hasan Akash, Mohammad Yeasin, Karl Van Horsen, Mithul Sathish, Susan Immanuel, Sanku Mallik
abstract: In a perfusion bioreactor, fresh culture medium enters through a small opening, flows through a collagen plug, and leaves through a second opening. How much pressure is needed to sustain that flow? When fresh medium reaches the outlet, has it also replaced the old medium inside the pores? To answer these questions, we simulated flow and medium replacement in pores traced from a collagen image. The flow simulations and curved-channel theory show how narrow, winding passages concentrate resistance. We used that resistance to estimate the plug permeability and found that the modeled plug accounts for most of the pressure drop across the chamber. Feeding through small openings adds to that demand because the flow must spread through the plug and converge again at the outlet. At the same flow rate, this requires about seven times the pressure needed with uniform feeding across the plug faces. Pore shape also affects how closely the outlet signal tracks replacement in the interior. In most runs, the interior reaches 99% replacement before the outlet does. A slowly exchanging side pocket can reverse that order by retaining old medium while fresh medium passes through the main channel. In the strongest case, the interior takes nearly three times as long as the outlet to reach the same replacement threshold.

infographic.key_insight: Narrow, winding collagen pores drive pressure demand, while slowly exchanging side pockets can make outlet measurements overstate internal medium replacement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Bioreactor design should account for inlet–outlet geometry and pore-level retention when sizing pumps and assessing medium renewal.
method: Simulated flow and medium replacement in pores traced from a collagen image.
Combined flow simulations with curved-channel theory to estimate resistance and plug permeability.
Compared small-opening versus uniform feeding and outlet versus interior replacement times.
infographic.evidence_signal: Small-opening feeding required about seven times the pressure of uniform feeding at the same flow rate; in the strongest side-pocket case, interior 99% replacement took nearly three times as long as outlet replacement.
infographic.watch_item: Results reflect modeled image-derived pores; broader experimental validation is needed before applying these pressure and replacement ratios to other collagen plugs.
infographic.paper_title: Pressure demand and solute replacement in a collagen-plugged bioreactor

title: Remote and Noncontact Acceleration and Suppression of Heat Convection on Object Surfaces using Intensity-Adjusted Acoustic Streaming
authors: Yuki Yuzawa, Keisuke Hasegawa
abstract: The temperature of objects in an environment is often controlled by accelerating or suppressing heat convection. Conventional methods generally involve insulation for heat retention and forced convection for cooling. However, there is no practical method for remotely and target-selectively controlling heat convection in objects in room environments. In this study, we demonstrated that intensity-adjusted acoustic streaming (ultrasound-driven airflow) can both suppress natural convection and induce forced convection on the surface of a heat source. The direct acceleration and deceleration of air over the object surface were induced by an ultrasonic beam with high temporal and spatial resolution. The experiment showed that it is possible to switch between insulating and cooling by adjusting the ultrasonic output intensity, and that it is essential for heat retention to prevent heat from escaping from the object surface by convection using acoustic streaming. We consider these results to lead to the realization of a situation where virtual heat-retaining blankets or cooling fans that are customized for specific objects in the environment can be ubiquitously attached to them, opening the door to applications such as temperature control of food and beverages and remote control of temperature profiles in manufacturing processes and laboratory settings.

infographic.key_insight: Adjusting ultrasound-driven airflow can remotely switch a heated object's surface between suppressed natural convection for heat retention and enhanced convection for cooling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Target-selective, noncontact convection control could enable localized temperature management for food, beverages, manufacturing, and laboratory processes.
method: Direct an ultrasonic beam at a heat-source surface to generate acoustic streaming.
Adjust ultrasonic output intensity to accelerate or decelerate near-surface airflow.
Switch between heat-retaining and cooling conditions without contacting the object.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments demonstrated intensity-dependent switching between heat retention and cooling, though the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Practical operating ranges, energy efficiency, and robustness to ambient airflow remain unspecified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Remote and Noncontact Acceleration and Suppression of Heat Convection on Object Surfaces using Intensity-Adjusted Acoustic Streaming

title: Azimuthally Resolved Energy Dissipation Rates in the Impingement Zone of Equal Free Impinging Liquid Jets: A Three-Dimensional Model
authors: Robert J. Demyanovich
abstract: When two equal liquid jets collide, they form a thin sheet of liquid and lose some of their incoming kinetic energy (doi:10.1615/AtomizSpr.2025056396). Calculating the energy dissipation rate per unit mass requires estimating the volume of the region where the collision takes place. This paper develops a three-dimensional model of that region and uses it to calculate how the energy dissipation rate varies with angular position within the collision region. The model assumes that the thickness of the collision region varies linearly along each radial line from the stagnation point to its outer boundary. Combining the resulting volume with the kinetic energy lost during the collision provides equations for both the overall energy dissipation rate and the rate averaged over each narrow angular portion of the collision region (local energy dissipation rate). For equal jets with uniform inlet velocity profiles, the model predicts substantial differences in energy dissipation rate with angular position, even when the incoming jets and the resulting sheet have uniform mean velocities. The model also reproduces expected theoretical limits, including a cylindrical collision region for directly opposed jets. Preliminary micromixing results are consistent with the predicted variation, although independent validation of the assumed collision-region geometry and the location of energy dissipation is still needed.

infographic.key_insight: A three-dimensional model predicts substantial angular variation in energy dissipation within equal-jet collisions, even with uniform inlet and sheet mean velocities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Resolving angular differences in dissipation could help engineers assess mixing conditions in impinging-jet devices beyond a single overall dissipation rate.
method: Model collision-region thickness as varying linearly along radial lines from the stagnation point to the boundary.
Combine modeled volume with collision-induced kinetic energy loss to calculate dissipation per unit mass.
Calculate overall and narrow-angular-sector-averaged dissipation rates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model recovers expected theoretical limits, including a cylindrical collision region for directly opposed jets, and preliminary micromixing results are consistent with its predicted angular variation.
infographic.watch_item: The assumed collision-region geometry and the actual location of energy dissipation still require independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: Azimuthally Resolved Energy Dissipation Rates in the Impingement Zone of Equal Free Impinging Liquid Jets: A Three-Dimensional Model

title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish
authors: Harry Walden, Ashutosh Tripathi, Teo Lara, Brandon Weissbourd, Jörn Dunkel
abstract: Fluid flows enable and limit the feeding and locomotion of sea creatures across a wide range of scales. Although much is known about how microorganisms navigate life at low Reynolds numbers, the effect of inertial flows on the feeding-efficiency of larger marine organisms remains less well understood. Here, using jellyfish as an archetypal example, we study the trade-off between prey capture rate and energy expended to generate inertial flows by surface deformations. We develop a feeding-efficiency landscape that predicts an optimal feeding regime at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, mediated by a self-generated vortex ring. These predictions provide a unifying biophysical explanation of size and beat frequencies reported for jellyfish species from different taxa, with vortex-ring-dominated transport supported by our experimental observations for the moon jellyfish \textit{Aurelia aurita}. More broadly, our results demonstrate how centimetric marine predators can exploit inertial flows for efficient prey capture.

infographic.key_insight: Jellyfish feeding efficiency is predicted to peak at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, where self-generated vortex rings enhance prey capture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings could guide bioinspired underwater pumps and robots that use pulsating surfaces to transport particles efficiently.
method: Study prey capture relative to the energy spent deforming the body surface.
Develop a feeding-efficiency landscape spanning Stokes pumping and inertial transport.
Compare predictions with reported jellyfish sizes and beat frequencies and observe flows around moon jellyfish.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predictions explain reported sizes and beat frequencies across jellyfish taxa, while experiments on Aurelia aurita support vortex-ring-dominated transport.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative efficiency gains or validation range, limiting direct engineering design guidance.
infographic.paper_title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish
